questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent. Calder & Wynn, a consumer law firm that sells fixed-fee legal services online (wills, trademark filings, tenant demand letters) and monthly legal plans, is building a support resolution agent with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles refund requests, billing disputes, and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), and the target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

To cut latency, a developer proposes a change to the loop: when a response arrives with stop_reason "tool_use" for lookup_order, the backend runs the tool, formats the order record as a chat message, and sends it directly to the client, ending the turn without another call to Claude. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Accept it for read-only tools such as lookup_order, and keep sending results back to Claude only for tools that change state, such as process_refund.
Reject it, because the tool result must be appended to the conversation and sent back to Claude, which keeps deciding until stop_reason is "end_turn".
Accept it, and add a system prompt note telling Claude which tool results are shown to clients directly, so its later replies stay consistent.
Reject it, and have Claude request every tool it may need in its first response instead, so one iteration covers lookup, refund, and reply.
questoes.explicacao: In the agentic loop, stop_reason "tool_use" means Claude is waiting for the tool result: you execute the tool, append the result to the conversation history, and send the next request so the model can reason about it. The loop ends only when Claude returns "end_turn". Short-circuiting after a tool call removes the model from exactly the step where it decides whether the order is refundable, needs clarification, or must be escalated.
feedbacks: Tempting because read-only calls feel harmless, but side effects are not the issue: after lookup_order, Claude still has to interpret the record and decide what to tell the client or which tool to call next. Skipping that step breaks the loop for the most common tool.
Correct. A "tool_use" stop means the loop must continue: run the tool, append the tool_result to the history, and call Claude again until it returns "end_turn".

Documenting the shortcut in the prompt does not restore the missing step. Claude never sees the result in the turn where it would decide what to do with it, so the client still gets a raw record instead of an answer.

This replaces model-driven decisions with a pre-planned sequence. Claude cannot know which tools it needs before seeing the order record; the loop still has to return results so the model can reason about them.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, the support agent is being split into a coordinator plus two subagents defined with AgentDefinition: billing-investigator and matter-status. Both definitions have clear descriptions and their own tool lists. In testing, the coordinator never delegates: it handles billing disputes itself with get_customer and lookup_order, and sometimes writes "I'll ask our billing specialist" before replying without any subagent running. Its configuration includes allowedTools: ["get_customer", "lookup_order", "escalate_to_human"]. Without changing the subagent definitions, what is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Add "Task" to the coordinator's allowedTools, since subagents are spawned through the Task tool and the coordinator has no way to invoke them now.
Add the subagents' tools, including process_refund, to the coordinator's allowedTools so that it can complete billing disputes without delegating.
Add a section to the coordinator's system prompt that names both subagents and says billing disputes must always go to billing-investigator.
Pass the coordinator's conversation history to both subagents at startup, so they already share the case context before work is handed to them.
questoes.explicacao: In the Agent SDK, subagents are spawned through the Task tool, and allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke them. Here the AgentDefinitions are fine, but the coordinator's allowed tools only cover direct lookups, so delegation is impossible however the prompt is written.
feedbacks: Correct. Subagents are invoked through the Task tool, and a coordinator can only call tools listed in its allowedTools. Without "Task" there, the definitions exist but can never be spawned.
This turns the coordinator into a generalist with more tools and does not enable delegation at all; it gives up the specialization the subagents were created for and makes tool selection harder.
A prompt instruction cannot make the coordinator call a tool it is not allowed to use. The "I'll ask our billing specialist" text shows the intent; what is missing is the mechanism, the Task tool.
Context must indeed be passed explicitly once a subagent is invoked, but that does not explain why no subagent is ever spawned. The blocker is the missing Task tool.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, before opening a billing dispute the agent extracts a dispute record (invoice_number, disputed_amount, service_date) from the documents clients attach: firm invoices with itemized tables, card statement excerpts, and forwarded emails such as "you billed me twice for the $349 trademark search." The prompt describes each field in detail, yet disputed_amount comes back null in 17% of disputes, even though a reviewer finds the amount in the document every time. Which TWO changes are most likely to fix this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Use few-shot examples whose answers first note where the amount was found (e.g., "second sentence of the email"), then give the record.
Replace the field descriptions with a longer paragraph that lists every place where a disputed amount can appear in client documents.
Make disputed_amount non-nullable in the extraction schema, so the model can no longer return a dispute record without an amount.
Add few-shot examples that all use the firm's standard invoice layout, so the model learns one consistent place to look for the amount.
Add few-shot examples in different layouts (itemized invoice, card statement line, narrative email), each with the correctly filled record.
questoes.explicacao: Few-shot examples are the most effective fix when fields that do exist in the source come back empty because documents vary in format. The examples should cover the different structures (tables, statement lines, narrative text) and can show where the value was found, so the model generalizes instead of matching a single layout. Forcing the field to be required would invite fabricated values.
feedbacks: Correct. Examples that first note where the value was located demonstrate the reasoning behind the extraction, which helps the model generalize to layouts the examples do not cover.
The prompt already describes the fields in detail and still yields inconsistent results. When instructions alone are not enough, concrete examples are more effective than more prose.

Tempting because it forces a value, but requiring a field the model cannot locate pushes it to fabricate one. The problem is finding the amount in unfamiliar layouts, not permission to leave it empty.
Examples are the right tool, but identical examples only teach the layout that already works. The nulls come from statements and emails, which these examples would not cover.
Correct. The nulls come from layouts the model does not handle; examples covering each document structure show how the same field appears in different formats.

questoes.pergunta: Calder & Wynn's malpractice insurer requires that process_refund never runs on an order whose matter_status is "filed" (the work was already submitted to a court or agency); those requests must go to a partner. Two designs are on the table: (1) a hook that intercepts every process_refund call, checks matter_status, blocks filed matters, and redirects to escalate_to_human; (2) a system prompt rule with six few-shot examples, which complied in 497 of 500 test transcripts. Which design should you choose?
opcoes: Design 1, because the insurer's rule has to hold on every call, and an interception hook enforces it regardless of what the model decides.
Design 2, because the model must understand the rule to explain it to clients, and a hook blocks the call without giving a reason it can relay.
Design 2, because 99.4% compliance in testing shows the prompt is reliable, and a hook would add a status lookup to every refund attempt.
Design 1, implemented as a PostToolUse hook that reverses refunds issued on filed matters, so valid refunds are never delayed by a check.
questoes.explicacao: Hooks give deterministic guarantees; prompt instructions give probabilistic compliance. When a business rule must hold every time, as with this insurer requirement, choose a hook that intercepts process_refund before it executes and redirects the case to escalation. The 0.6% failure rate in testing is the reason to do so, not an argument against it.
feedbacks: Correct. When a business rule requires guaranteed compliance, a hook that intercepts the outgoing tool call gives a deterministic guarantee; prompt instructions, even with examples, leave a non-zero failure rate.

Tempting, but it assumes a hook is opaque. A blocking hook can return a reason ("matter already filed; route to a partner") that the model uses in its reply, so you get both enforcement and an explanation.

Three violations in 500 is exactly the non-zero failure rate that prompt-based compliance leaves. For a rule the insurer requires every time, "usually" is not enough, and one status lookup is a small cost.

A PostToolUse hook runs after the refund was already issued, so it detects the violation instead of preventing it, and reversals can fail. Compliance rules are enforced by intercepting the call before it executes.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, the agent adds an internal note for the finance team whenever it sees a billing problem; the instruction is "Flag any unusual charges on the client's account." Finance now receives about 60 flags a day, mostly legitimate rush fees, court filing fees, and prorated plan charges, and has started ignoring the queue. Finance wants flags only for real billing errors. What should you change in the prompt?
opcoes: Add a second review prompt that checks whether each flagged charge is truly unusual before the note reaches the finance team's queue.
Ask the agent to score each potential flag from 1 to 10 for how likely it is an error, and send finance only flags that score 8 or higher.
Flag a charge only if it differs from the price on the signed order, or if the same service is billed more than once in a billing period.
List the legitimate charge types finance sees most often (rush fee, filing fee, proration) and tell the agent never to flag those types.
questoes.explicacao: Vague instructions such as "flag unusual charges" produce false positives because the model has to invent its own definition of a problem. Explicit criteria that state what to report (amount differs from the signed order, duplicate billing) improve precision far more than confidence thresholds or extra review layers, and protect finance's trust in the flags.
feedbacks: A second pass that applies the same vague notion of "unusual" inherits the same ambiguity, and adds cost. The missing piece is a definition of what counts as an error.
Confidence-based filtering does not define what counts as an error, and self-assigned scores are not calibrated. Finance may simply receive fewer of the same wrong flags.

Correct. Explicit, checkable criteria (the amount differs from the signed order; the same service is billed twice) replace a vague instruction and tell the agent exactly what to report, which is what raises precision.

A skip list helps with today's noise but still leaves "unusual" undefined: any legitimate charge not on the list (a new fee, a discount reversal) would still be flagged. It says what to ignore, not what to report.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, two transcripts were escalated in the same week. In the first, the payment processor timed out during process_refund, and the agent told the client that the refund was "declined under firm policy." In the second, the refund was refused because the order was outside the 30-day refund window, and the agent retried process_refund four times before apologizing for "a technical problem." What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The system prompt does not tell the agent how to respond to a failed tool call, so it improvises a different explanation for every failure.
process_refund reports every failure the same way, with no error category or retry flag, so the agent cannot tell a timeout from a policy denial.
The MCP server does not set isError on failed calls, so the agent reads the failure text as a normal result and invents a reason for it.
The agent has too many tools available, which makes it unreliable at choosing between retrying process_refund and calling escalate_to_human.
questoes.explicacao: When a tool returns the same generic failure for every case, the agent cannot make the right recovery decision. Structured error metadata (an errorCategory such as transient vs business, an isRetryable boolean, and a human-readable description) lets the agent retry the timeout and explain the window violation to the client instead of retrying it.
feedbacks: Tempting, but better prompt instructions cannot help the agent react correctly if the tool result looks the same for both failures. The agent needs information that distinguishes them, not more guidance.

Correct. With a uniform error, the agent cannot know that the timeout is transient and retryable while the window violation is a business error that must not be retried. Structured metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable, a readable description) fixes both behaviors.

If isError were missing, the agent would treat the calls as successful, but it clearly recognized both as failures: it retried one and apologized for the other. The issue is what the failure says, not whether it is flagged.
Too many tools does degrade selection, but this agent has four and chose process_refund correctly. Its mistake is in interpreting the failure, which points to the error response itself.

questoes.pergunta: The Calder & Wynn engineers who build the support agent use Claude Code with a shared MCP server for the firm's case-management API. The original developer added it with a command that stored it in her ~/.claude.json, and the three engineers who joined this month do not have it, so Claude Code cannot query test matters in their sessions. Each engineer has their own API token. Which TWO changes should you make? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Ask each new engineer to run the command the original developer used, so the server is added to each engineer's own ~/.claude.json file.
Have the server configuration read the API token from ${CASE_API_TOKEN}, an environment variable each engineer sets on their own machine.
Keep the server at user level and add a setup step to the README, since servers that use credentials belong in user configuration.
Move the server definition into a .mcp.json file at the repository root and commit it, so every engineer gets the server when they pull.
Commit a single shared service-account token in the server configuration, so every engineer can authenticate without any extra setup steps.
questoes.explicacao: MCP scoping follows who needs the server: project-level .mcp.json for shared team tooling, user-level ~/.claude.json for personal or experimental servers. A server the whole team needs goes in the committed .mcp.json, with ${VAR} expansion so each engineer provides their own token without secrets in the repository.
feedbacks: This works for today's three engineers but keeps the configuration personal and unversioned; every future hire must repeat the step, and configurations drift apart. Shared tooling belongs at project level.
Correct. Environment variable expansion (${VAR}) keeps the shared configuration free of secrets, so it can live in version control while each engineer uses their own token.

Tempting because of the tokens, but credentials are handled with ${VAR} expansion in the project file. User level (~/.claude.json) is for personal or experimental servers, not for one the whole team needs.
Correct. Project-scoped .mcp.json is the place for shared team tooling: it is versioned with the repository, so new engineers get the same server configuration automatically.
This puts a secret in version control and makes every engineer act under one identity. ${VAR} expansion avoids both while keeping the configuration shared.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, lookup_order returns {"orders": []} both when a client has no orders in the requested period and when the orders database query times out. During a 40-minute database incident, the agent told 23 clients that "we have no record of any purchase from you," and two of them filed chargebacks. Which TWO changes to lookup_order's responses best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Return isError true whenever no orders are found, so that the agent always confirms with the client before saying no purchase exists.
Keep the empty list in both cases, and tell the agent in its prompt to treat any empty result as a possible outage and to offer escalation.
On a timeout, return an error result with isError true, a transient category, and isRetryable true, instead of an empty orders list.
Retry the query inside lookup_order until it returns at least one order, so a temporary outage never reaches the agent as an empty list.
When the query succeeds with no matches, return a successful result stating the criteria searched, so the agent can treat it as an answer.
questoes.explicacao: Access failures and valid empty results must look different to the agent. A timeout should come back as a structured error (isError, transient, retryable) so the agent can make a retry decision; a successful query with no matches should come back as success, ideally with the criteria searched, so the agent can treat it as a real answer.
feedbacks: Marking a successful query with no matches as an error is the mirror-image mistake: a valid empty result is information, and treating it as a failure triggers needless retries and confirmations.
The tool would still hide the distinction, and the agent would now treat genuine "no orders" answers as possible outages, escalating clients who simply bought nothing in that period.
Correct. A timeout is an access failure: the agent needs to know the query did not run, so it can retry or tell the client it cannot check right now, instead of stating there is no purchase.
A client who really has no orders would make this loop never end. Retrying until something comes back confuses a valid empty result with a failure.

Correct. A successful query with no matches is a valid empty result. Returning it as success, with the criteria searched, lets the agent answer confidently and keeps it distinct from the failure case.

questoes.pergunta: Calder & Wynn's human support staff work in a separate ticketing system and never see the agent's conversation. For mid-process handoffs, a developer proposes this escalate_to_human payload: {"customer_id": "C-48213", "customer_name": "Dana Ruiz", "contact_email": "dana.ruiz@example.com", "conversation_summary": "Client is unhappy with a charge on her trademark order and wants a human."} How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Approve it, because with the customer details staff can trace the root cause in the billing system, and a short summary is quick to read.
Approve it, but require conversation_summary to be at least 300 words, so the agent includes all the details the client gave in the chat.
Extend it with the root cause found, the amount involved, what was already checked, and a recommended action, so staff can act at once.
Replace conversation_summary with the full transcript of the chat, so staff can read exactly what the client and the agent said before acting.
questoes.explicacao: A mid-process escalation should use a structured handoff that includes customer details, the root cause the agent established, and the recommended action, plus relevant amounts and what was already checked. Staff who do not see the transcript can then act immediately instead of repeating the investigation. Customer identity plus a vague summary is not enough.
feedbacks: Customer details are necessary but not sufficient. Staff would have to redo the investigation the agent already did, because the summary says nothing about what is wrong or what should be done.
A longer free-text summary adds length, not structure. Staff still have to dig out the root cause and the next step, and the content will vary from one escalation to the next.
Correct. A structured handoff protocol carries customer details, the root cause analysis, and the recommended action, so staff who lack the transcript can act without re-investigating.

Tempting because nothing is lost, but staff do not work from the conversation, and a raw transcript leaves them to reconstruct the analysis. The handoff should deliver the conclusions in a structured form.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, the agent assigns a priority (P1, P2, P3) to every escalated ticket so staff know which to handle first. The prompt says "P1 = urgent, P2 = important, P3 = routine." An audit of 200 tickets found the same situation, a client with a court filing deadline in two days, labeled P1 in 54% of cases and P2 or P3 in the rest. The team can change the prompt but cannot add new services. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Define what qualifies a ticket for each priority, with two or three concrete example tickets per level, e.g., a filing deadline within 72 hours for P1.
Ask the agent to rate urgency on an explicit 1–10 scale and map score ranges to priorities, so the finer scale gives more precise decisions.
Describe the firm's practice areas and typical matter timelines in the prompt, so the agent understands which kinds of ticket are truly urgent.
Have the agent classify each ticket three times and assign the priority that appears most often, so that isolated misclassifications drop out.
questoes.explicacao: Inconsistent classification comes from undefined levels. Explicit criteria for each severity or priority level, illustrated with concrete examples of what belongs in each, are the most effective way to get consistent labels. Finer scales, extra background, or voting do not define the boundaries between levels.
feedbacks: Correct. Labels such as "urgent" are interpreted differently from case to case. Explicit criteria for each level, illustrated with concrete examples, give the agent a consistent standard to apply.
A finer scale moves the ambiguity instead of removing it: without a definition of what makes a ticket urgent, the 1–10 score will vary just as much as P1–P3 did.
More background can help the agent reason, but it still leaves the boundary between levels undefined, so the same deadline can still land in different priorities.
Voting hides inconsistency without fixing its cause, and triples the calls. If the criteria are ambiguous, the majority label can still be wrong for a whole class of tickets.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, a client disputed two charges. The agent refunded the first ($180, within its limit), found that the second ($1,240) required staff approval, and called escalate_to_human with the note "Billing dispute, client needs help." A staff member, who cannot see the conversation, reviewed the account and refunded both charges, so the client received $180 twice. Four similar double refunds happened this month. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add a hook that blocks process_refund for the rest of a ticket once escalate_to_human has been called, so no refund can follow an escalation.
Instruct staff to check the payment system for refunds issued in the last 24 hours before acting on any escalated billing ticket.
On escalation, pass a structured summary: customer ID, root cause, refunds already issued, amount still disputed, and recommended action.
Stop the agent from issuing any refund on tickets with more than one disputed charge, so that staff handle all of those charges together.
questoes.explicacao: When escalating to humans who lack the conversation transcript, the agent should compile a structured handoff summary: customer ID, root cause, amounts including actions already taken, and the recommended action. Here, the missing information about the refund already issued directly caused the duplicated work.
feedbacks: The duplicate refund was issued by a staff member, not by the agent after escalating, so this hook would not have prevented it. The problem is what the staff member knew.
This pushes the reconstruction work onto staff and relies on a manual check every time. The agent already knows what it did; it should hand that over.

Correct. Staff lack the transcript, so the handoff must carry the facts they need: who the client is, what was found, what was already done ($180 refunded), what remains ($1,240), and what the agent recommends.
This avoids double refunds by giving up first-contact resolution on every multi-charge dispute, including the part the agent handled correctly. The gap is in the handoff, not in the refund.

questoes.pergunta: One Calder & Wynn engineer wants to try a community MCP server that queries public court calendars, to see whether it could help the support agent answer deadline questions. Nobody else on the team has asked for it, and it may be dropped after a week. He is deciding where to configure it for his own Claude Code sessions. Which option is best?
opcoes: Add it to the project .mcp.json, so that the experiment is visible to the whole team and its configuration gets reviewed in a pull request.
Write a thin custom MCP server around the court-calendar API instead, so the team controls the code before anyone starts to depend on it.
Add the server to his personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so that only his own sessions connect to it and the team's files stay unchanged.
Add it to his user-level ~/.claude.json, which makes it available in his own sessions without changing the team's shared setup.
questoes.explicacao: Configure personal or experimental MCP servers in user-scoped ~/.claude.json, and shared team tooling in project-scoped .mcp.json. An experiment one engineer is evaluating should not change everyone else's sessions; if the team adopts the server later, it moves to the project file.
feedbacks: Visibility is nice, but a project-level entry gives the server to every teammate who pulls, for an experiment nobody else asked for. The shared .mcp.json is for team tooling.

A custom wrapper is extra work for an experiment that may be dropped in a week, and existing community servers are preferred for standard integrations. It also leaves open where to configure the server.
The personal scope is right but the file is wrong: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md holds personal instructions, not MCP server configuration, so mentioning the server there does not connect it.

Correct. Personal or experimental MCP servers belong in user-scoped ~/.claude.json: available to him across projects, invisible to the team, and easy to drop. If it proves useful, it can move to .mcp.json later.

questoes.pergunta: Calder & Wynn's agent loop ends when the last text block of a response contains words such as "resolved" or "anything else", or after 6 iterations. In 5% of tickets, the conversation ends while a process_refund call requested in that same response is never executed, and long billing disputes are cut off at the sixth iteration mid-investigation. Which TWO changes should you make to the loop's control flow? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Raise the iteration cap from 6 to 15, so that long billing disputes can finish before the loop stops the conversation.
Continue whenever stop_reason is "tool_use": execute the requested tools, append their results, and send the next request.
End the loop when stop_reason is "end_turn", whatever the text says, keeping a high cap only as a safety net.
Match the closing phrases only in the final sentence of the response, so phrases quoted earlier do not end the loop.
End the loop when a response contains a text block and no tool call, since that text is the agent's reply to the client.
questoes.explicacao: Agentic loop control flow should be driven by stop_reason: continue while it is "tool_use", executing tools and appending their results, and terminate when it is "end_turn". Parsing phrases, checking for text, and using an arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stop are the anti-patterns behind both symptoms.
feedbacks: A higher cap delays the cut-off but keeps an arbitrary iteration count as the main stopping mechanism; some disputes will still be cut off, and the skipped-refund bug remains.
Correct. stop_reason "tool_use" means Claude is waiting for tool results; the loop must run the tools, append the results to the history, and continue, even when the same response also contains text.

Correct. "end_turn" is the signal that Claude has finished; terminating on it, rather than on text content, is the reliable stopping condition. A cap may remain as a safeguard, not as the primary mechanism.
Refining the phrase match is still parsing natural language to decide termination. Claude can write "anything else?" in the same response in which it requests a tool.
Checking for assistant text is a listed anti-pattern. Text without a tool call also appears when a response is cut off by max_tokens, and the check is indirect; stop_reason is the explicit signal.

questoes.pergunta: At Calder & Wynn, get_customer comes from the CRM's MCP server and returns plan_start as a Unix timestamp (1717200000); lookup_order comes from the billing MCP server and returns order_date in ISO 8601 and payment_status as a numeric code (3 = chargeback open). Audits show the agent sometimes says a 20-day-old order is outside the 30-day refund window, and it once offered a refund on an order with payment_status 3. The refund policy is stated clearly in the prompt. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: The 30-day rule exists only in the system prompt, so the agent applies it inconsistently from ticket to ticket; it should be enforced in code.
Earlier tool results are dropped from the conversation history between turns, so the agent reasons about dates it no longer has in view.
Raw results from different MCP servers reach the model in mixed date and status formats that it misreads; they should be normalized first.
Order records contain dozens of fields the agent does not need, which dilutes its attention so that it overlooks the dates that matter.
questoes.explicacao: Heterogeneous formats from different MCP tools (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, numeric status codes) are a common source of reasoning errors. A PostToolUse hook can intercept each tool result and normalize these values before the model processes them, so date arithmetic and status checks work on consistent data.
feedbacks: Enforcing the window in code would help for that one rule, but the agent also misreads a payment status code; both errors come from how the data arrives, not from how the policy is phrased.
If results were dropped, the agent would lack the dates altogether or ask for them again. Here it has the values and misinterprets them.

Correct. Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and numeric codes from different servers are easy to misread. A PostToolUse hook that converts them to one format (ISO dates, readable status names) before the model sees them removes the source of these errors.
Verbose results do waste context, but trimming fields would leave the Unix timestamp and code 3 in place, and those are exactly what the agent misreads.

questoes.pergunta: Calder & Wynn's identification flow for the agent is: (1) call get_customer with the name and email the client provides; (2) if several records match, select the one with an open matter, since clients usually contact support about active work; (3) call lookup_order for that customer; (4) if a refund is due and under $300, call process_refund, otherwise escalate. In a pilot, two clients named Alex Chen who share a family email address received each other's order details. Which step contains the flaw?
opcoes: Step 1, because get_customer should be called with an order number rather than a name and email, since order numbers are always unique.
Step 4, because process_refund should require staff approval for any amount, so that a misidentified client never receives a refund.
Step 2, because picking the record with an open matter is a heuristic; the agent should ask for another identifier, such as a matter number.
Step 3, because lookup_order should run before get_customer, so the order the client mentions determines which customer record is used.
questoes.explicacao: Multiple matches require clarification, not heuristic selection. Choosing the record with an open matter, the most recent activity, or any other guess will sometimes pick the wrong person, which here exposed another client's data. The agent should ask for an additional identifier before proceeding.
feedbacks: Order numbers can help, but clients often do not have one at hand, and step 1 is reasonable. The failure happens when several records match and the agent picks one by guesswork.
Requiring approval for every refund would sacrifice first-contact resolution and still not fix the data exposure: the wrong client already saw order details at step 3.

Correct. When a lookup returns multiple matches, the agent should ask for an additional identifier (matter number, phone, billing ZIP code) instead of selecting a record by a heuristic such as "has an open matter."
Reordering does not resolve the ambiguity: the client may not give an order number, and identity must still be established before account data is shared.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code. Nestwell runs a real-estate listings portal (property search, a mortgage calculator, dashboards for agents). Its developers use Claude Code for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation, and are integrating it into their workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configuration, and clear guidance on when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

The team added .claude/rules/listing-sql.md with the frontmatter paths: ["services/listings/**/*.sql"]. Its conventions are applied when Claude edits services/listings/migrations/0042_add_hoa_fee.sql, but not when it edits db/shared/views/listing_summary.sql, which also queries the listing tables. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: Path-scoped rules are loaded at the start of every session, so the model saw the rule in both cases and simply did not follow it for the shared view.
The ** in the paths glob matches only a single directory level, so the rule covers files directly inside services/listings/ but no nested files.
The rule loads only when Claude works on files matching its glob; the shared view is outside services/listings/, so the rule never loads for it.
Rules in .claude/rules/ take effect only for files listed in an @import of the root CLAUDE.md, and the shared view is not among the listed files.
questoes.explicacao: Files in .claude/rules/ with a paths frontmatter of glob patterns load only when Claude edits matching files, which keeps irrelevant conventions out of context. Here the glob covers only services/listings/, so the shared view never triggers the rule; widening the glob (or adding the other location) fixes it.
feedbacks: Rules with a paths field are conditional: they load only when Claude works with matching files, which is how they save context. Blaming the model misses that the rule was never loaded for that file.
** matches any number of directory levels; that is why the migration under services/listings/migrations/ did get the rule. The shared view fails because it is outside services/listings/ entirely.

Correct. A paths glob limits when the rule loads. To cover listing SQL wherever it lives, add the other location (e.g., "db/shared/**/*.sql") or use a pattern that matches the files regardless of directory.
Rule files are discovered from .claude/rules/ without being imported, and path-scoped ones activate by glob. @import is a CLAUDE.md mechanism for including other files, not a switch for rules.

questoes.pergunta: At Nestwell, Claude Code wrote a migration script that converts legacy listing prices stored as text into a numeric price column. Legacy values include "$450,000", "450K", "Contact agent", empty strings, and NULL. After two rounds of asking Claude to "handle the edge cases properly", NULL still becomes 0 and "Contact agent" crashes the script. A teammate proposes writing a detailed paragraph that explains how each kind of edge case should be treated. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: a precise written specification is the clearest way to define edge-case behavior, and it can be reused for the next migration.
Prefer test cases with concrete inputs and expected outputs, e.g., NULL → price NULL with price_on_request true, "450K" → 450000.
Reject it and switch to plan mode, so Claude can explore the legacy table and propose its own handling of each edge case first.
Reject it: handle the edge cases by hand in a small pre-processing step, and keep Claude's script for values that parse cleanly.
questoes.explicacao: When natural-language descriptions produce inconsistent edge-case handling, give Claude specific test cases with example inputs and expected outputs, such as how NULL values must be migrated. Concrete pairs are unambiguous and verifiable, which is why they work better than more prose.
feedbacks: Prose has already been interpreted inconsistently twice. More prose may help, but concrete input/expected-output pairs remove the ambiguity that descriptions leave.
Correct. Specific test cases with example input and expected output (NULL, empty string, "Contact agent", "450K") show exactly how each edge case must be handled and can be run to verify the fix.
Plan mode is for architectural or multi-file decisions; this is one script whose expected behavior the team already knows. Exploration does not tell Claude which output you want.
Pulling the edge cases out by hand works around the problem instead of communicating the requirement, and leaves two code paths to maintain for a single migration.

questoes.pergunta: At Nestwell, a developer is using Claude Code to build a mortgage affordability calculator with well-defined rules: down payments from 0% to 50%, 10- to 40-year terms, HOA fees, property tax by county, and a 200 ms response budget. Each round of feedback fixes one problem and breaks something that worked before; after five rounds she is still finding regressions by hand. The requirements are stable. What is the most effective way to proceed?
opcoes: After each change, ask Claude in the same session to review its own code against the requirements before she tests the result by hand.
Rewrite the requirements as one complete message and ask Claude to regenerate the calculator from scratch so all rules apply together.
Switch to plan mode and have Claude design the calculator's architecture before it makes any more changes to the implementation.
Write a test suite first, covering expected results, edge cases, and the 200 ms budget, then iterate by sharing failing tests.
questoes.explicacao: With stable, well-defined requirements, write the test suite first (expected behavior, edge cases, performance) and iterate by sharing test failures with Claude. Each round is then verified against everything that already worked, which ends the cycle of regressions found by hand.
feedbacks: Self-review in the same session is weak because Claude keeps the reasoning that produced the code, and she would still be finding regressions by hand.
One detailed message helps when issues interact, but regenerating from scratch gives no way to detect what broke; the regressions would return on the next round.
The architecture is not the problem: the rules are clear and stable. What is missing is an automatic check that earlier behavior still holds.

Correct. Test-driven iteration fits stable, well-defined requirements: the tests capture expected behavior, edge cases, and performance, every round is checked automatically, and failing output gives Claude precise feedback.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell's GraphQL resolvers live in nine service directories (services/*/graphql/*.resolver.ts) and in an older admin package outside services/. Their conventions (use the shared DataLoader; check the agent's role before returning contact details) are in a CLAUDE.md inside services/search/graphql/, so Claude follows them there but not when it edits resolvers in other services. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add a CLAUDE.md to every graphql/ directory that @imports one shared resolver-conventions file, so the text lives in a single place.
Move the conventions to a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.resolver.ts"], so they load whenever Claude edits any resolver.
Move the conventions into the root CLAUDE.md, so that Claude has them in context in every session, whatever directory it works in.
Move the CLAUDE.md up to services/, one level above the service directories, so that it covers the graphql/ folders of all nine services.
questoes.explicacao: For conventions that apply to a file type spread across many directories, a .claude/rules/ file with a glob pattern beats directory-level CLAUDE.md files: one source of truth that loads automatically for every matching file and stays out of context otherwise.
feedbacks: Sharing one file via @import avoids duplicated text, but it is still directory-bound: ten CLAUDE.md files to maintain, and any new service directory is missed until someone adds another one.
Correct. A path-scoped rule with a glob by file type applies the conventions to every resolver regardless of directory, including the admin package, and loads only when a resolver is being edited.
This applies the conventions, but loads resolver rules into every session, including frontend and infrastructure work, which wastes context on irrelevant instructions.
Moving the file up covers the nine services but still misses the admin package outside services/, and it loads resolver conventions for every file under services/, not just resolvers.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell is replacing the mapping library in its property search UI; about 50 files use the old library's map, marker, and clustering APIs, and the new library handles clustering differently. One developer wants to do the whole migration in direct execution because the target library is already chosen; another wants to stay in plan mode for the entire task. Which approach should the team take?
opcoes: Direct execution throughout, since the library decision is already made and the remaining work is mechanical replacement, file by file.
Plan mode throughout, approving each file's change inside plan mode so that nothing is modified without a reviewed design for that file.
Direct execution, with a prompt that asks Claude to list every affected file first and then edit all of them in that same pass.
Plan mode to explore usages and agree on an approach, including clustering, then direct execution to apply the agreed plan.
questoes.explicacao: Large migrations combine both modes: plan mode to explore the codebase and settle the approach (here, how clustering will work with the new library) before committing to changes, then direct execution to carry out the planned edits efficiently.
feedbacks: The library choice is made, but the clustering difference is a design decision that touches many files. Editing before investigating it risks costly rework in the middle of the migration.
Plan mode is for exploring and designing before changes; using it for the whole implementation adds friction to the part of the work that becomes well defined once the plan is agreed.
Listing the files first is a step toward investigation, but it skips agreeing on how clustering should be handled before 50 files are edited.
Correct. Combine the two: plan mode to investigate and design a migration that involves real decisions, then direct execution to implement the approved approach.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell's team guideline says "Always start Claude Code in plan mode." Developers complain that one-line fixes, such as adding a null check to a single function with a clear stack trace, now take several extra minutes, and some have started ignoring the guideline altogether, including for multi-service work. The team wants a guideline that keeps the benefits of plan mode where they matter. What should the new guideline say?
opcoes: Keep plan mode for every task, but let developers approve short plans without reading them whenever a change looks small enough.
Use direct execution by default and rely on code review to catch problems, switching to plan mode only after a change causes rework.
Decide by file count alone: plan mode when a change will touch more than ten files, and direct execution for everything below that.
Plan mode for multi-file changes, architectural decisions, or several valid approaches; direct execution for well-scoped fixes.
questoes.explicacao: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications; direct execution suits simple, well-scoped changes. A guideline built on these criteria keeps planning where it prevents rework without slowing down one-line fixes.
feedbacks: Rubber-stamping plans keeps the overhead and removes the benefit. The guideline should distinguish tasks by complexity instead of hiding the cost.
Waiting for rework before planning gives up what plan mode is designed for: exploring and designing before committing to large or architectural changes.

File count is one signal, but a three-file change that requires choosing between integration approaches still needs planning. The decision depends on complexity and on whether several approaches are valid, not on one threshold.

Correct. Plan mode is designed for complex tasks: large-scale or multi-file changes, architectural decisions, several valid approaches. Simple, well-scoped changes such as a single null check suit direct execution.

questoes.pergunta: A Nestwell tech lead created a /listing-audit command last week and uses it every day. Two teammates pulled the main branch this morning; for them, /listing-audit does not exist, while other team commands such as /new-endpoint work normally. The tech lead also notices that /listing-audit is available when she opens unrelated repositories on her laptop. What is the most likely root cause?
opcoes: Commands are cached when a session starts, so her teammates need to restart Claude Code after pulling before the new command appears.
The command file has no description in its frontmatter, so Claude Code registers the command only for the person who created the file.
New commands have to be referenced in the project CLAUDE.md before Claude Code makes them available to the other developers on a team.
The command file is in her user-level ~/.claude/commands/ directory, which is personal and is not shared through the repository.
questoes.explicacao: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ are shared through version control; user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ are personal and available in all of that user's projects. A command that appears in unrelated repositories but not for teammates lives in the user directory.
feedbacks: A restart may be needed for some changes, but it would not explain why the command also shows up in her unrelated repositories. That points to where the file lives.
Frontmatter descriptions help with discovery but do not make a command personal. Who sees a command depends on the directory, not on the file's metadata.
CLAUDE.md does not register commands. The teammates already see /new-endpoint without any CLAUDE.md reference, which rules this out.
Correct. A command that follows her into every repository lives in ~/.claude/commands/. To share it with the team, it must be in the repository's .claude/commands/ directory and committed.

questoes.pergunta: At Nestwell, Claude Code generated a new search ranking function, and a developer found four problems: (a) the price filter runs before currency conversion, so euro-priced listings are filtered by their raw numbers; (b) conversion is applied after pagination, so page sizes come out uneven; (c) a log message has a typo; (d) a unit test has a misleading name. Her plan is to send one message per problem, in that order, waiting for each fix before the next. What is the flaw in this plan?
opcoes: All four problems belong in one message: even independent problems take longer to fix one at a time than when described together.
The filter and conversion problems interact and belong in one detailed message; only the independent ones suit sequential fixes.
Each fix should be requested in a separate fresh session, so the context of earlier fixes cannot influence how Claude handles the next.
She should first ask Claude to find all problems on its own, instead of listing the ones she found, so that none of them are missed.
questoes.explicacao: Put interacting issues in a single detailed message so Claude can design one consistent fix, and iterate sequentially on independent issues. Here the filter and pagination problems both depend on where conversion happens, while the typo and the test name are independent.
feedbacks: Batching everything is not the rule. Independent problems such as a typo and a test name are fine to fix one at a time; the problem is sending the interacting ones separately.

Correct. When fixes interact (both change where conversion happens relative to filtering and pagination), separate rounds make each fix undo or conflict with the other. Interacting issues go in one detailed message; independent ones can be iterated sequentially.
Fresh sessions would lose useful context and do not address the real issue: two fixes that depend on each other would still be made in isolation.
Asking Claude to look for more issues can be useful, but it does not change the fact that the known interacting problems must be handled together.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell's monorepo has four packages (web, mobile, pricing-engine, mls-ingest) and a docs/standards/ folder with accessibility.md, money-handling.md, api-errors.md, and geo-data.md. Today the root CLAUDE.md @imports all four standards, so Claude loads accessibility rules while working on the pricing engine and occasionally applies web conventions in mls-ingest. Which TWO changes best fit this situation? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Keep importing all four standards from the root CLAUDE.md, and add a sentence telling Claude to apply only the parts that fit the package.
Remove the four @import lines from the root CLAUDE.md, and keep only the conventions there that genuinely apply to every package in the repo.
In each package's CLAUDE.md, @import only the standards its maintainers consider relevant, e.g., pricing-engine imports money-handling.md.
Move the four standards files into each developer's ~/.claude/ directory, so every developer loads them in all of their Claude Code sessions.
Copy the relevant sections of each standards file into each package's CLAUDE.md, so that every package's instructions are self-contained.
questoes.explicacao: Use @import in each package's CLAUDE.md to include only the standards files relevant to that package, based on the maintainers' domain knowledge, and keep the root CLAUDE.md for conventions that apply everywhere. Each standard lives in one file, packages import what they need, and irrelevant conventions stay out of context.
feedbacks: Relying on Claude to infer which imported rules apply is what produces the current mix-ups, and all four files still consume context in every session.

Correct. The root CLAUDE.md should hold only what applies everywhere; taking the four imports out of it stops every session from loading every standard, while package-level imports bring in what each package needs.
Correct. Package-level CLAUDE.md files that @import only the relevant standards use the maintainers' knowledge of what each package needs and keep unrelated rules out of context.
User-level files are not shared through version control and would load every standard in every project, the opposite of selective inclusion.
Copying text gives each package the right content today but creates duplicates that drift when a standard changes. @import keeps one source per standard.

questoes.pergunta: At Nestwell, Claude Code reviews pull requests before human review. A recent PR touched 23 files to change listing prices from dollars to integer cents. The single-pass review gave detailed comments on the first files, missed that two dashboard components still divided by 100, and contradicted itself about the same rounding helper. The tech lead proposes reviewing each file in its own pass and posting the combined per-file findings. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt per-file passes, and add a separate integration pass that follows the price field across files, which per-file passes cannot see.
Adopt it as proposed: with one independent pass per file, each file gets full attention, so problems like the dashboard division are caught.
Reject it, keep the single pass, and put a summary of the PR's intent at the top of the prompt so the review knows what to check in each file.
Adopt it, giving each per-file pass the full diff of the other 22 files as reference, so that cross-file effects are visible in every pass.
questoes.explicacao: Large multi-file reviews should be split into focused per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow. Per-file passes alone miss bugs that exist only between files, such as consumers that were not updated when a producer changed units.
feedbacks: Correct. Per-file passes fix the uneven depth and the contradictions, but the dashboard bug is a cross-file data-flow problem (a producer changed units, its consumers did not). A separate integration pass is needed for that.
Per-file passes solve attention dilution, but each pass sees only one file. The dashboard components look correct in isolation; the bug appears only when you follow the price field across files.
Putting the intent first helps with position effects, but the review still processes 23 files at once, which is what caused the uneven depth and contradictory findings.
Attaching the other 22 diffs to every pass re-creates the dilution the split was meant to remove. Cross-file analysis belongs in one dedicated integration pass.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell has a /dependency-report skill that inspects lockfiles across 30 packages and prints several hundred lines of version and license details before its final summary. Developers run it in the middle of feature work; afterwards Claude tends to lose track of the feature it was building, and its later answers drift. Developers want to keep running the skill mid-task and still see its summary. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Add context: fork to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter, so it runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only its result returns.
Tell developers to run /compact right after each use of the skill, so the verbose output is condensed before they continue working.
Add allowed-tools to the skill's frontmatter, limiting it to Read and Grep, so the skill can no longer generate as much output.
Move the skill's instructions into the project CLAUDE.md as explicit standards, so the checks are always in context and the skill is unneeded.
questoes.explicacao: The context: fork frontmatter option runs a skill in an isolated sub-agent context, which keeps verbose skill output out of the main conversation. The main session receives only the result, so the developer's ongoing task keeps its context.
feedbacks: Correct. context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, so the hundreds of lines of intermediate output never enter the main conversation; the developer still receives the summary.
/compact reduces context after the fact by replacing the history with a summary, which can also compress details of the feature work the developer wants to keep. It treats the symptom on every run.
allowed-tools restricts which tools the skill can use; it does not control how much output those tools put into the conversation. Read and Grep can still produce hundreds of lines.
CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards. Moving an on-demand report there adds permanent context and does not stop the report's output from flooding the session.

questoes.pergunta: At Nestwell, Claude Code's automated review produces about 60 findings per week. Only two senior engineers can verify findings, and together they have time for roughly 15. Last quarter they labeled 300 past findings as valid or invalid. The team wants to send the seniors the findings most likely to be wrong while still posting the others. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Add a verification pass that gives each finding a confidence, set thresholds using the 300 labeled ones, and route low scores to the seniors.
Change the review prompt to report only high-confidence findings, so the weekly volume falls to what the two seniors can actually verify.
Run the review three times on each pull request and send the seniors only those findings that do not appear in all three runs.
Send the seniors a random sample of 15 findings each week, and use their verdicts to estimate the overall precision of the review.
questoes.explicacao: A verification pass in which the model reports confidence alongside each finding enables calibrated review routing: thresholds tuned on labeled findings send uncertain findings to humans and let the rest flow through. This differs from asking the model to "only report high-confidence findings", which filters instead of routing and is not calibrated.
feedbacks: Correct. A verification pass in which the model self-reports confidence alongside each finding, with thresholds calibrated against the labeled findings, sends limited reviewer time where errors are most likely.
"Only report high-confidence findings" is a vague filter that does not reliably improve precision, and it hides findings instead of routing them, so the seniors' expertise is not used where it helps.
Inconsistency across runs is a weak and costly proxy for error, and it triples the review cost. It also provides no calibrated estimate of which findings are wrong.
Random sampling is good for measuring the overall error rate, but it does not direct attention to the findings most likely to be wrong, which is what the team wants.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell's root CLAUDE.md has grown to 1,400 lines covering testing, API conventions, deployment, and accessibility. Four different owners edit it, merge conflicts happen every week, and developers struggle to find the section they should update. The team is choosing between keeping a single file, restructured with a table of contents and strict headers, and splitting it. Which design is the best choice?
opcoes: One file with a table of contents and strict headers, which keeps all conventions in one place so that Claude can apply them consistently.
Topic files in .claude/rules/ (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md...), each kept by its owner and path-scoped where useful.
Topic files in each developer's ~/.claude/rules/, so that every owner can update their topic without causing merge conflicts in the repo.
Topic directories such as testing/ and deployment/ at the repo root, each holding its own CLAUDE.md, so that every topic loads separately.
questoes.explicacao: The .claude/rules/ directory lets you split a large CLAUDE.md into focused topic files (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md). The configuration becomes modular and easier to maintain, and individual rule files can be path-scoped when a topic applies only to certain files.
feedbacks: A table of contents helps navigation but keeps four owners editing one file; the merge conflicts and the monolith problem remain.

Correct. .claude/rules/ is designed for organizing topic-specific rule files as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md. Each owner maintains a focused file, and rules can later be scoped with paths where they apply only to certain files.
User-level files are not shared through version control, so teammates would stop receiving the conventions altogether.
A directory-level CLAUDE.md loads when Claude works in that directory; testing conventions apply to code throughout the repo, not to files inside a testing/ folder.

questoes.pergunta: Nestwell's developers rely on several Claude Code skills during feature work, and the team is deciding which skills should declare context: fork in their SKILL.md frontmatter. Each skill is described below by what it does when invoked mid-task. Which TWO skills are the best candidates? Choose TWO.
opcoes: /route-inventory: scans all 400 route files and produces a long inventory of their endpoints, handlers, and middleware.
/compare-layouts: drafts and critiques eight alternative layouts for the listing page before the developer picks one to build.
/commit-message: writes a commit message that summarizes the changes Claude made to the code during the current conversation.
/fix-review: applies the review comments that the developer and Claude agreed on earlier in the current session to the open files.
/explain-error: explains the stack trace the developer pasted a few messages ago, in the context of the code that was just changed.
questoes.explicacao: context: fork isolates skills that produce verbose output (codebase scans) or exploratory context (brainstorming alternatives) from the main session. Skills that depend on the current conversation, or whose short output is tied to it, should stay in the main context.
feedbacks: Correct. A scan of 400 files produces verbose output; isolating it keeps the main conversation clean and returns only the inventory or a summary.
Correct. Brainstorming alternatives creates exploratory context the main session does not need; running it in a fork keeps only the chosen direction or a summary.
A commit message must reflect what happened in this conversation; isolating the skill from the conversation removes the information it needs.
This skill depends on the discussion in the current session. A forked context starts isolated from that conversation, so it would not know which comments were agreed.
Explaining an error pasted earlier relies on the main conversation's context, and its output is short; forking it gains nothing and loses the context.

questoes.pergunta: At Nestwell, Claude Code must change the searchable flag on 6 of the 40 field definitions in config/listing-fields.ts, where every definition has the same shape (name, type, searchable: false, facet: false). Its Edit calls on this file keep failing, and it keeps retrying with slightly different short snippets, while its edits to other files in the same session succeed. What is the most likely cause, and what should Claude do instead?
opcoes: The file is too large for Edit to process in one call; Claude should first split the configuration into several smaller modules.
Edit matching is sensitive to indentation; Claude should reformat the file to consistent spacing and then retry the same Edit calls.
A build watcher rewrites the generated file between calls; Claude should stop the watcher and then retry the Edit calls on the file.
Edit needs anchor text that occurs only once, and the repeated blocks offer none; Claude should Read the full file and then Write it.
questoes.explicacao: Edit makes targeted changes by matching unique text; in a file with many identical blocks, short snippets match several places and the edit fails. When Edit cannot find unique anchor text, use Read to load the full file contents and Write to save the modified version.
feedbacks: Splitting the file is a refactor nobody asked for, and size is not what defeats Edit here; 40 short definitions make a small file.
Whitespace can break a match, but then the snippet would not be found at all. With 40 identical blocks, short snippets match many places, and no reformatting creates a unique anchor.
Nothing suggests the file is generated or rewritten, and edits elsewhere succeed. The pattern points at the file's repeated content.
Correct. Edit makes targeted changes using unique text matching. When the text to change is not unique, the reliable fallback is Read to load the full file, then Write the modified version.

questoes.pergunta:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System. The Revenue Policy Office of a national tax agency is building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents (one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, one generates reports), and the system produces comprehensive, cited reports for policy analysts.

The web search subagent runs this loop: send the messages; if stop_reason is "end_turn", stop; otherwise execute the requested search_web calls, write their results to an audit log, and replace the history with two messages, the original task and "Searches done, continue.", to keep requests small. Logs show the subagent repeating the same queries and ending with "no relevant sources found." What is the flaw?
opcoes: The loop stops on "end_turn" rather than after a fixed number of searches, so the subagent can keep searching without any limit.
The original task is resent in every request; it should be sent once, since the model keeps it from the loop's first request.
Writing the results to an audit log exposes them twice, which confuses the model about which queries were already completed.
The search results are never added to the messages as tool results, so each request lacks the data that earlier searches found.
questoes.explicacao: Between iterations of the agentic loop, tool results must be appended to the conversation history so the model can incorporate them into its reasoning. Replacing the history with the task and a status line throws the results away, which produces repeated searches and false "nothing found" conclusions.
feedbacks: Terminating on "end_turn" is correct; switching to a fixed number of searches would make an arbitrary cap the stopping mechanism. The repetition has a different cause.
The API is stateless: each request must carry everything the model should see. Resending the task is required, not a flaw.
The audit log is written by the application and never sent to the model, so it cannot confuse it. Logging is fine.

Correct. Tool results must be added to the conversation (as tool_result blocks following the assistant's tool_use) between iterations. Dropping them means Claude never sees what it found, so it searches again and concludes that nothing was found.

questoes.pergunta: At the tax agency's research system, the document analysis subagent returns its findings to the coordinator as prose paragraphs with inline mentions such as "(see the 2023 OECD review, p. 14)". In recent reports, 18% of citations point to the wrong document or lack a page number, although spot checks show the underlying findings are accurate. Which statement about this behavior is correct?
opcoes: Citations should be added at the end by the report subagent from a structured source list, since synthesis rewrites findings and loses them.
Citations are lost because subagents do not share memory; letting synthesis read the analysis subagent's history would preserve them.
The analysis subagent is inventing sources, so a separate verification subagent should re-check every citation before synthesis starts.
Content and sources mixed in prose come apart; structured records (claim, document, URL, page) keep each claim tied to its source.
questoes.explicacao: When context passes between agents, use structured formats that separate content from metadata such as source URLs, document names, and page numbers. In free prose, attribution is implicit and gets lost or misattached when synthesis recombines findings.
feedbacks: Adding citations at the last step, even from a structured source list, means matching claims to sources after the link between them has already been lost; the report generator would have to guess. Attribution must travel with each finding from the start.
Subagents indeed do not inherit each other's context, but the fix is to pass information explicitly in a format that preserves attribution, not to hand synthesis another agent's whole history.
Spot checks show the findings are accurate, so the sources exist. A verification layer adds cost without fixing how attribution is carried between agents.
Correct. Passing findings as structured data that separates content from metadata (source URL, document name, page number) lets downstream agents keep each claim attached to its source.

questoes.pergunta: At the tax agency's research system, the document analysis subagent receives a package of 38 public-consultation responses on a proposed carbon border levy and analyzes them in one pass. Its output covers the first responses in depth, summarizes later ones in a line each, and states two contradictory conclusions about the same exemption. A teammate proposes three passes over the full package: one for rate proposals, one for exemptions, and one for administrative burden. How should you evaluate this proposal?
opcoes: Adopt it: aspect-focused passes give each task a specific focus, so every pass can give all 38 responses the attention one pass could not.
Split by document instead: analyze each response in its own pass, then run a separate cross-document pass to compare and reconcile them.
Adopt it, and add a final pass that re-reads only the responses that got short summaries, so that their coverage reaches the same depth.
Keep a single pass, but put a list of all responses with section headers at the top, so the model gives the later responses equal weight.
questoes.explicacao: Large reviews should be split into per-item local passes plus a separate integration pass to avoid attention dilution. Splitting by aspect still processes every document at once, so the dilution persists; splitting by document and then integrating gives consistent depth and one place to reconcile findings across documents.
feedbacks: Each aspect pass still reads all 38 responses at once, so the attention dilution that caused uneven depth and contradictions remains, now three times over.

Correct. Per-document local passes give each response consistent depth; a separate integration pass then compares positions across responses and resolves contradictions, instead of asking one pass to do both over 38 documents.
Patching the shallow summaries afterwards treats a symptom; the contradictory conclusions come from analyzing everything together, which this keeps.
Headers and ordering mitigate position effects, but they do not reduce the load of analyzing 38 documents in one pass, which is the source of the shallow and contradictory output.

questoes.pergunta: At the tax agency's research system, every request runs the full pipeline: web search, document analysis, synthesis, and report generation. Requests such as "turn last week's report on remote-worker withholding into a one-page brief for the minister" therefore trigger new searches and a full re-analysis, take 25 minutes, and sometimes cite sources that were not in the original report. Broad research questions must keep full coverage. What is the most effective fix?
opcoes: Add a classifier model in front of the coordinator that deterministically assigns each request to one of two fixed pipelines, full or short.
Run the four subagents in parallel instead of in sequence, so requests that do not need every stage still finish much more quickly.
Have the coordinator assess what each request needs and invoke only those subagents, e.g., only report generation for a reformat.
Cache every finished report with its sources, and return the cached report whenever a new request mentions the same policy topic.
questoes.explicacao: Coordinators should analyze each request and dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline. This cuts latency and cost on narrow requests and avoids side effects such as new sources entering a document that should only be reformatted.
feedbacks: A separate classifier adds infrastructure and still forces requests into fixed pipelines; the coordinator can already analyze each request and decide which subagents it needs.
Parallelism cuts wall-clock time but still runs unnecessary stages, and the stages depend on each other (synthesis needs search and analysis results). New sources would still leak into the brief.

Correct. A coordinator should analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke. A reformat request needs only the report generator working from the existing report, while broad questions still use the full pipeline.
Caching may help repeated questions, but a request to condense a report still requires new work, and matching by topic risks serving stale or mismatched reports.

questoes.pergunta: At the tax agency's research system, a report stated that "no court rulings on the tax treatment of crypto staking rewards were found." An analyst later discovered that the case-law database had timed out on 3 of the 5 queries the search subagent sent; for those queries, the subagent returned an empty results list, exactly as it does when a query finds nothing. What is the most effective first step?
opcoes: Have the search subagent report timed-out queries as access failures, separately from the queries that completed with no matches.
Instruct the synthesis subagent to avoid statements of absence such as "no rulings were found" in any of the reports it writes.
Have the coordinator re-run every search whose results list is empty, as a separate step before the findings go on to synthesis.
Increase the case-law database timeout from 10 to 30 seconds, so that complex queries have enough time to complete normally.
questoes.explicacao: Distinguish access failures (timeouts, which need retry decisions) from valid empty results (successful queries with no matches). When both look like an empty list, the coordinator draws false conclusions of absence; reporting failures explicitly lets it retry or flag the gap.
feedbacks: Correct. An access failure (timeout) and a valid empty result (the query ran and nothing matched) mean different things. Reporting them distinctly lets the coordinator retry the failed queries and keeps genuine "none found" results trustworthy.
This also suppresses valid conclusions: when a query really finds nothing, that is a useful finding. The problem is that the coordinator cannot tell the two cases apart.
Re-running every empty result wastes work on queries that legitimately have no matches, and still cannot tell a second timeout from a real empty answer.
A longer timeout may reduce how often this happens, but any future timeout will still be reported as "no results" and produce the same false conclusion.

questoes.pergunta: At the tax agency's research system, the coordinator spends several turns with an analyst agreeing on scope: data from 2019–2024, OECD member countries only, excluding sub-national taxes. It then delegates to the search and analysis subagents with prompts such as "Research digital services tax revenue." The results include 2016 data, non-OECD countries, and city-level levies. Which design should the team adopt?
opcoes: Configure the subagents to run inside the coordinator's session, so the scope agreed with the analyst becomes available to them automatically.
Add the scope rules (years, OECD only, no sub-national taxes) to each subagent's AgentDefinition system prompt as explicit standing rules.
Have the coordinator write the agreed scope (years, countries, exclusions) explicitly into the prompt of every Task call it makes.
Pass the coordinator's entire conversation with the analyst to each subagent, so they can read the full scope discussion themselves.
questoes.explicacao: Subagents operate with isolated context: they do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history. Anything they need, such as the scope agreed with the analyst, must be written explicitly into the prompt the coordinator sends with each Task call.
feedbacks: Subagents run with isolated context and do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history; no setting makes the agreed scope appear in their context automatically.
Standing constraints in the AgentDefinition apply to every request. This scope was negotiated for this request, and the next analyst may want different years or countries.
Correct. Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history, so the coordinator must provide the relevant context explicitly in each subagent's prompt.

This passes context explicitly, but sends a long negotiation instead of its outcome. Subagents must extract the scope themselves, which wastes context and risks misreadings; give them the agreed constraints directly.

questoes.pergunta: At the tax agency's research system, the coordinator spawns four parallel web search subagents for "digital services taxes in Europe", each with the same prompt. The four result sets overlap by about 70%, the same 12 sources are cited by all four, and coverage of trade disputes and compliance costs is thin. Which TWO changes best address this? Choose TWO.
opcoes: Have the coordinator split the topic into non-overlapping subtopics and state each one's boundaries in that subagent's Task prompt.
Keep the identical prompts, and have the synthesis subagent remove duplicated sources before it combines the four sets of findings.
Give each subagent a different search engine, so that the four result sets come from different indexes instead of the same one.
Give each subagent a distinct type of source, e.g., legislation databases, official statistics, academic papers, and news.
Replace the four subagents with one search subagent that has four times the search budget, so that no source is retrieved twice.
questoes.explicacao: The coordinator should partition research scope across subagents, by subtopic or by source type, so parallel agents cover distinct ground. Identical prompts produce duplicated work and leave parts of the topic uncovered; cleaning up afterwards does not recover the missing coverage.
feedbacks: Correct. Partitioning the topic into non-overlapping subtopics, with the boundaries stated in each Task prompt, gives each subagent distinct ground, minimizing duplication and giving thin areas dedicated effort.
Deduplication cleans the output but does not recover the coverage lost to overlapping work; trade disputes and compliance costs stay thin.
Different engines still rank the same prominent sources highly, and every subagent keeps the same goal; overlap persists because the scope itself was never divided.
Correct. Partitioning by source type is another way to split the scope: each subagent covers different ground, so the results complement rather than repeat each other.
One agent avoids duplication but gives up parallelism and still has no plan for covering the subtopics evenly.
